domain: Comparative Law / Constitutional Pluralism / Religious Governance
topic_summary: Analysis of India's simultaneous maintenance of Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi, and secular personal law regimes governing marriage and family matters within a single constitutional state. The system has persisted for decades without zero-sum displacement, raising the question of whether this represents one contested kernel (marriage/family law authority) read through multiple religious-cultural lenses, or multiple distinct kernels coexisting without shared substrate.

key_entities: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 (codified Hindu personal law)
Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 (Islamic family law framework)
Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872 (Christian marriage/divorce rules)
Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936 (Zoroastrian community law)
Indian Constitution Article 44 (Directive Principle: uniform civil code aspiration)
Supreme Court of India (constitutional arbiter; periodic UCC advocacy)
key_tensions: Religious community autonomy vs constitutional uniformity (personal law boards vs Article 44 advocates)
Gender equity standards vs religious law preservation (Shah Bano case; triple talaq debate)
Secular state authority vs religious interpretive authority (who adjudicates family disputes)

omegas.description: Is this ONE kernel (marriage/family authority) read five ways, or FIVE distinct kernels with no shared substrate? The D2 culture-level break suggests incoherent bundle, but 75 years of coexistence without zero-sum displacement suggests shared constitutional substrate. Generation will test whether readings share axioms about state authority vs community autonomy.
omegas.source: §1.3-K kernel/not-kernel decision; flagged as strongest D2 case in research context

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition applied per §1.3-K. Five readings selected based on distinct institutional authority structures (Hindu codified statute, Muslim personal law boards, Christian canonical courts, Parsi community tribunals, secular civil code). Each reading instantiates different interpretive authority grounding. Axiom contradiction testing deferred to generation step per protocol.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The legitimacy basis for adjudicating marriage validity, divorce, inheritance, and custody within the Indian constitutional framework
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Contested: religious community boards claim interpretive authority grounded in scriptural/traditional law; secular state claims authority grounded in constitutional uniformity and individual rights

readings.commitment: Marriage/family law authority derives from codified Hindu law (Hindu Marriage Act 1955) as interpreted by civil courts
readings.authority_grounding: State codification of religious tradition; parliamentary sovereignty
readings.expected_structural_delta: Uniform rules within Hindu community; state courts adjudicate; moderate gender equity (better than Muslim, worse than secular)

readings.commitment: Marriage/family law authority derives from Shariat as interpreted by Muslim personal law boards and qazis
readings.authority_grounding: Religious law autonomy; community self-governance; colonial-era recognition
readings.expected_structural_delta: Community tribunals adjudicate; lower gender equity (unilateral talaq, polygamy, inheritance); state intervention contested

readings.commitment: Marriage/family law authority derives from Christian canonical law as codified in Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872
readings.authority_grounding: Denominational church authority mediated through colonial-era statute
readings.expected_structural_delta: Restrictive divorce (fault-based); church tribunals for annulment; moderate gender equity

readings.commitment: Marriage/family law authority derives from Parsi community custom as codified in Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936
readings.expected_structural_delta: Community tribunals; endogamy enforcement; high gender equity within community; demographic decline threatens viability

readings.commitment: Marriage/family law authority derives from secular civil code (Special Marriage Act 1954) grounded in constitutional individual rights
readings.authority_grounding: Constitutional secularism; individual autonomy; opt-in rather than default
readings.expected_structural_delta: Civil courts adjudicate; highest gender equity; inter-religious marriage enabled; social costs for exit from community law

axiom_contradictions.basis: Shariat reading grounds authority in divine law interpreted by religious scholars (no single coherent framework can hold both 'divine law is supreme' and 'individual constitutional rights are supreme' as simultaneously true foundational axioms)

Hindu reading accepts state codification and parliamentary amendment of religious law; Muslim reading rejects state authority to modify Shariat (no framework holds both 'state can revise religious law' and 'religious law is immune to state revision' as simultaneously true)

Canonical reading grounds marriage indissolubility in sacramental theology; secular reading grounds marriage as civil contract dissolvable by mutual consent (no framework holds both 'marriage is ontologically indissoluble' and 'marriage is a revocable contract' as simultaneously true)
